title: Premio dialoghi a carrère
lead: Pistoia, 3 giugno. Lo scrittore francese Emmanuel Carrère ha ricevuto ieri a Pistoia il premio Dialoghi, che "ha ridefinito i confini della letteratura contemporanea". Il premio è stato consegnato durante la manifestazione "Il libro in piazza".
corpo1: Emmanuel Carrère, noto per le sue opere che sfidano i confini tra letteratura e giornalismo, ha ricevuto il premio Dialoghi a Pistoia. Il premio è stato istituito per riconoscere opere letterarie innovative e ha già onorato autori di fama Internazionale. La manifestazione "Il libro in piazza" è un evento culturale importante che riunisce lettori e scrittori da tutta Italia. Secondo la giuria del premio, Carrère ha "ridefinito i confini della letteratura contemporanea" con le sue opere, che combinano elementi di romanzo, saggio e giornalismo.

        The "Il libro in piazza" format is the textbook example of how Italy manages culture: an event in the square, a few tents, and a high-profile name to validate the operation. Carrère, who has dismantled the wall between reality and fiction in works like Limonov or The Adversary, is the perfect guest for a system that loves "international prestige" but struggles to integrate these hybrid forms into its own academic or publishing circuits.
        The "Premio Dialoghi" carries a name that evokes the great classical tradition—Plato, Seneca—but in the current landscape of local cultural funding, these labels often serve as an aesthetic shield. When a prize is awarded for "redefining boundaries," it's important to ask who is actually redefining what. In Italy, the boundary being redefined is often just the one between genuine critical promotion and the need for a local administration to show a "cultural balance sheet" to the citizens.
        Carrère's work is a slap to the face of the "pure" Italian novelist who still believes in the sanctity of the plot. Yet, by placing him in the context of a square-based festival, the operation risks neutralizing the subversive nature of his non-fiction, transforming a radical literary practice into a mere "event."
        If the Italian cultural system continues to use international authors as trophies for local events without creating a structural space for the hybrid genres they represent, the "dialogue" promised by the award remains a monologue of the administration. The result is a cultural landscape where the prestige of the guest is used to mask the emptiness of the critical method, and this mechanism is precisely what allows provincialism to survive under the guise of cosmopolitanism.
